quote: His case for the third ... became the design argument of the ARPANET.
problem: p3 has just said the ARPANET was built so universities could share computers, "not to survive a war". Baran's case was survival, so a caption saying that case "became the design argument of the ARPANET" reads as if the war purpose came back, and the reader re-reads to work out which is true.
fix: separate shape from purpose, e.g. "his third shape became the ARPANET's shape, though not its purpose"
reason: Real tension. ch9-arpanet-p3 says ARPA built the network for sharing computers, 'not to survive a war', then the Fig 9.3 caption says Baran's survival case 'became the design argument of the ARPANET'. A careful reader has to work out which is true. Shape and purpose need separating. Keep the caption at two sentences.
judge_fix: Replace the caption's second sentence (ch9-arpanet-p5) with: "His third shape, packets finding their own way through redundant links, became the ARPANET's design, though survival was never its purpose."

quote: recomputes the checksum; the rest travels untouched
problem: The book has never said what a checksum is (Fig 8.11 only labels FCS as 'checksum'), so this reader cannot explain why a router has to recompute it after changing the TTL. The drawn 'TTL changed, so recompute the checksum', with 12849 becoming 13105, and the strip's 'covers only the header' have nothing to rest on.
fix: one clause: a number worked out from the header's bytes so the next router can spot damage; change a byte and it changes
reason: Checked part-1 to part-3: the only earlier uses are the bare label 'FCS: checksum' in Fig 8.11 and the disk-block bullet in Ch5. The book never says what a checksum is. The Fig 9.4 animation 'TTL changed, so recompute the checksum' and the strip's 'covers only the header' therefore have nothing to rest on. One clause in the Time to live strip bullet fixes it. Combine with finding 4, since both edit the same bullet.
judge_fix: In the Fig 9.4 strip, bullet 'Time to live', replace the last sentence 'The checksum covers only the header, so each hop recomputes it.' with: "The header checksum is a number worked out from the header's bytes, so damage shows up; change the TTL and it changes too, so each hop recomputes it. It covers the header only."

quote: lowers the time to live by one
problem: Nothing says why a packet should have a lifetime at all. The strip only says a router drops it at 0 and that traceroute uses this, so this reader may conclude TTL exists for traceroute. p1's 'when to drop it' is never tied to it.
fix: so a packet sent round in circles by a routing mistake dies instead of looping forever
reason: The strip says only that the TTL drops by one, that a router drops the packet at 0, and that traceroute uses this. Nowhere does the book say why a packet needs a lifetime, so the reader may take traceroute to be the purpose. The glossary entry has the same gap. Combine with finding 3 in the same bullet.
judge_fix: In the same strip bullet, open with: "The **TTL** drops by one at every hop, so a packet sent round in circles by a routing mistake dies instead of looping forever; if it reaches 0 the router drops the packet and reports back, which is how `traceroute` maps a path: probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 make each hop answer in turn." Then the checksum sentences from finding 3.

quote: IPv6 forbids router-side fragmentation entirely.
problem: The paragraph has just made splitting the only way a too-big packet can cross a smaller link, then forbids it. It never says what an IPv6 router does with a packet that does not fit, and the strip's 'Path MTU discovery finds the smallest link' does not say how a sender can learn the size of links on a route it cannot see.
fix: the router drops it and tells the sender 'too big, the limit is N'; the sender resends smaller packets (path MTU discovery)
reason: p3 makes splitting the only way a too-big packet crosses a small link, then says IPv6 forbids it. The strip's 'Path MTU discovery finds the smallest link' is a slogan: a sender cannot see links on a route it does not control, and the book never says how it learns the limit. Law 4 rules out the slogan. One clause in the strip is enough. Leave p3 alone.
judge_fix: In the Fig 9.5 strip, bullet 'Avoiding it', replace with: "Path MTU discovery finds the smallest link on the route: a router that cannot pass a packet drops it and tells the sender the limit, and the sender resends smaller packets."

quote: Google is AS 15169, your ISP has its own
problem: ISP is never expanded anywhere in the book. Up to here the text says only 'internet provider' (ch8-substrates-p6 and Fig 8 caption), yet Fig 9.7 hangs every label on the acronym ('your ISP', 'regional ISP'), so the reader has to guess what it stands for.
fix: expand it once at first use: 'your internet provider (ISP)'
reason: Checked: the first 'ISP' in the book is ch9-routing-p2 ('your ISP'). Ch8 used 'internet provider' (ch8-substrates-p6 and its caption) and the acronym is never expanded, yet Fig 9.7 labels hang on it. A small but real first-use gap. The fix is one parenthesis.
judge_fix: In ch9-routing-p2 change "your ISP has its own" to "your internet provider (ISP) has its own".

quote: each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table
problem: The reader knows a port only as a physical socket on a switch (ch8-ethernet); here it is a number written as 100.64.0.11:5000 or 'port 40001', and without knowing that every packet carries such a number for its conversation, the reader cannot see how one shared address gets each reply back to the right home (the NAT rewrites the sender to 203.0.113.5 port 40001, the server replies to that, and the table maps it back to home A).
fix: one clause: a port is a number in each packet naming its conversation, so a reply to port 40001 can be looked up and passed back to home A
reason: Before Fig 9.8 the book uses 'port' only for a physical socket on a switch (ch8-ethernet). Ports as numbers in a packet are first taught in Ch10 (UDP). The NAT mechanism (one address, a port per connection, a table mapping replies back) cannot be followed without that meaning. The caption is where the term is used, so the fix goes there.
judge_fix: Replace the caption clause with: "each outgoing connection given its own port (a number every packet carries to name its conversation) in a translation table, so replies find their way back to the right home." Keep the caption to two sentences.

quote: thousands of homes share one public address
problem: Each home in the figure still has an IPv4 address (100.64.0.11 and so on), so the reader cannot explain why those addresses do not use up the same scarce supply, or why the server could not just reply to them; the step left out is that the 'shared' 100.64 range is used again inside every ISP and never appears on the public internet.
fix: a phrase: the 100.64 addresses are reused inside every ISP and cannot be reached from outside, so only the one public address counts
reason: Each home in the figure still has a 100.64 IPv4 address, and the book never says why those do not consume the scarce public supply. RFC 6598 (April 2012) reserves 100.64.0.0/10 as shared address space for carrier-grade NAT. It is not globally routable, and every ISP may reuse it inside its own network. That one fact closes the gap. It belongs in the strip bullet 'The shared range', which also covers finding 11.
judge_fix: Fig 9.8 strip, bullet 'The shared range': "100.64.0.0/10 was set aside in 2012 for exactly this layer. Every ISP reuses it inside its own network and never lets it onto the public internet, so it uses up no public addresses and never collides with the 192.168 addresses of the home networks behind it." Source: RFC 6598.

quote: so a forged source gets through and any reply goes to the address it names
problem: The section never says what a forger gains from a packet whose reply it never sees (hiding who sent it, or aiming the replies at a victim). The figure even shows the reply going elsewhere, so the danger promised by "at your peril" stays abstract and the reason ISPs bother to filter (p1) is left unstated.
fix: one clause: the forger hides itself and the replies land on whoever owns the address it wrote
reason: The section and its figure never say what a forger gains from a packet whose replies it cannot see, so 'at your peril' stays abstract and the reason ISPs filter (p1) is unstated. The strip 'One way only' already says spoofing suits single packets and that SYN flood relies on it. Adding the two real motives (hide the sender, aim replies at a victim) there makes the danger concrete. The caption stays at two sentences.
judge_fix: Fig 9.10 strip, bullet 'One way only': "A forger never sees the reply, so it cannot hold a TCP conversation; spoofing suits single packets that need no answer, either to hide who sent them or to aim the replies at a victim, which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood relies on it."

quote: meant to block YouTube at home but leaked worldwide by its upstream PCCW
problem: p4 introduces hijacking as "a more dramatic attack", but its canonical example turns out to be a domestic block that escaped by mistake ("leaked"). Fig 9.12 then defines a route leak as a mistake where nobody attacked, so the reader cannot say what made 2008 a hijack and not a leak.
fix: one clause: a hijack is announcing addresses you do not hold, whether on purpose or by error; PCCW failed to filter it
reason: Real inconsistency. p4 introduces hijacking as 'a more dramatic attack' that 'exploits' BGP and calls 2008 the canonical example. The Fig 9.11 strip says 'No malice... a configuration mistake', and the Fig 9.12 caption defines a route leak as the case where 'nobody attacked anything'. The reader cannot tell why 2008 is a hijack and not a leak. Pakistan Telecom announced a prefix it did not hold (a hijack, here by error) and PCCW failed to filter it. The glossary already says 'an attack, or accident', so the body should match. Fix p4 (not owner text).
judge_fix: In ch9-security-p4 change the first sentence to "A more dramatic failure starts in BGP itself." and the last to: "This is *BGP hijacking*: announcing addresses you do not hold, on purpose or by mistake. The canonical example happened on *24 February 2008*."

quote: A forger never sees the reply, so it cannot hold a TCP conversation
problem: This contradicts the book's own Ch10 (ch10-attacks), which tells how Mitnick held exactly such a blind, spoofed TCP connection on Christmas Day 1994 by predicting the ISN, an attack Morris described in 1985. A reader of Ch10 meets the opposite claim one chapter later. It is hard only because sequence numbers are now random.
fix: "A forger never sees the reply, so unless it can guess TCP's sequence numbers (Chapter 10's Mitnick story) it cannot hold a conversation; spoofing suits single packets, which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood relies on it."
reason: Real internal contradiction. ch10-attacks tells how Mitnick held a blind, spoofed TCP session on Christmas Day 1994 by predicting the ISN, after Morris described it in 1985. Fig 9.10's strip says a forger 'cannot hold a TCP conversation', and a reader meets the opposite one chapter later.
judge_fix: Fig 9.10 strip, 'One way only': "A forger never sees the reply, so spoofing suits single packets, as in Chapter 10's SYN flood; holding a whole TCP conversation blind means guessing sequence numbers, which Mitnick managed in 1994."

quote: the outage came from a configuration mistake upstream, where PCCW passed its customer's announcement on without filtering it
problem: This puts the whole mistake upstream. In the RIPE NCC RIS case study, Pakistan Telecom (AS 17557) itself started the unauthorised announcement of 208.65.153.0/24 to its upstream, and PCCW (AS 3491) then spread it. The chapter's own hero lead says the opposite ('a misconfigured router in Pakistan'), so the reader gets two different culprits.
fix: "The block was a domestic order; the outage came from two configuration mistakes: Pakistan Telecom announced its block route to its upstream PCCW, and PCCW passed it on without filtering it." Source: ripe.net/publications/news/youtube-hijacking-a-ripe-ncc-ris-case-study.
reason: Confirmed against the RIPE NCC RIS case study (ripe.net/publications/news/youtube-hijacking-a-ripe-ncc-ris-case-study/). Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) announced 208.65.153.0/24 to its upstream PCCW (AS3491), which passed it on. The strip blames only the upstream. The hero lead and caption do not contradict it (they say Pakistan's block 'leaked'), so this is a precision gap and not a two-culprit clash.
judge_fix: Fig 9.11 strip, 'No malice': "The block was a domestic order; the outage came from two configuration mistakes: Pakistan Telecom let its blocking route escape to its upstream, and PCCW passed that customer announcement on without filtering it."

quote: somewhere between five thousand and ten thousand machines (by rough estimates, about ten percent of the internet
problem: The usual estimate is about 6,000 of the roughly 60,000 hosts then online (FBI 30th-anniversary account), and Stoll counted about 2,000. No source gives 10,000, and 10,000 would be a sixth of the internet, not 'about ten percent', so the sentence disagrees with itself.
fix: "about six thousand machines (by the usual rough estimate, a tenth of the sixty thousand then online)". Sources: FBI, 'The Morris Worm' (2018): 'an estimated 6,000 of the approximately 60,000 computers'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_worm.
reason: The range and the percentage disagree: 10,000 would be about a sixth of the roughly 60,000 hosts then online. The usual estimate is about 6,000, about a tenth (FBI, 'The Morris Worm' 2018; Spafford's report). Not on the UNDER.md ledger or the owner-ruling list; the Morris 'twenty-three' ruling is unrelated.
judge_fix: ch9-security-p2: replace "somewhere between five thousand and ten thousand machines (by rough estimates, about ten percent of the internet of the time)" with "about six thousand machines (by the usual rough estimate, a tenth of the internet of the time)".

quote: and weak passwords in rsh
problem: The rsh/rexec route used trusted-host logins that needed no password. Weak passwords were a separate route: the worm cracked the password file and logged in with what it guessed. Passwords are not 'in rsh'.
fix: "and the password-free trusted logins of rsh, helped by passwords it could guess". Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_worm (rexec/rsh 'with no password requirements'; dictionary attack on weak passwords).
reason: Weak passwords were a separate route (dictionary attack on accounts). The rsh/rexec route used trusted-host logins (.rhosts, hosts.equiv) with no password, and the book's own Ch10 describes rsh as granting login without a password. 'Weak passwords in rsh' is wrong on both counts. Sources: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_worm and RFC 1135.
judge_fix: ch9-security-p2: replace "and weak passwords in rsh" with "and the trusted-host logins of rsh, helped along by guessable passwords".

quote: Charley Kline, a graduate student in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA
problem: UCLA's alumni history lists him as 'Charley Kline '70, M.S. '71, Ph.D. '80', a student assistant. A 1970 bachelor's means he was an undergraduate in October 1969. Primary accounts (UCLA, the ARPANET record) call him a 'student programmer'.
fix: "Charley Kline, a student programmer in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA". Source: UCLA Alumni, 'UCLA History' (alumni.ucla.edu).
reason: Sources conflict on 'graduate student'. UCLA alumni history lists him as 'Charley Kline '70, M.S. '71', and Kleinrock-side accounts say 'student programmer'. 'Student programmer' is safe and costs nothing.
judge_fix: ch9-arpanet-p1: "Charley Kline, a student programmer in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA".

quote: The "LO" message was packet switching going live
problem: Two sentences earlier the same paragraph says Davies 'built a small working network at NPL by 1969'. The NPL Mark I was running in early 1969, before 29 October, so 'packet switching going live' contradicts the paragraph's own history.
fix: "The "LO" message was the ARPANET's packet switching going live, though ARPA built it ..." Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPL_network ('operational in early 1969 then fully operational in January 1970').
reason: Same paragraph says Davies built a small working network at NPL by 1969 (operational early 1969), then calls LO 'packet switching going live'. Two words fix it.
judge_fix: ch9-arpanet-p3: "The \"LO\" message was the ARPANET's packet switching going live, though ARPA built it to let universities share expensive computers, not to survive a war."

quote: thousands of homes share one public address
problem: Scale overclaim, by about ten times. One address has about 64,000 ports, and each outgoing connection takes one, as the figure itself shows. A home keeps hundreds of connections open, so CGNAT port blocks are typically 256 to 1,000+ ports per subscriber: tens to a few hundred homes per address. Thousands of homes share a CGNAT's pool of addresses, not one address.
fix: "dozens or even hundreds of homes share one public address"
reason: Overclaim. One address has about 64,000 ports and each connection takes one, as the figure shows, so fixed-line CGNAT typically puts tens to a few hundred subscribers on an address. 'Thousands' is too high. 'Hundreds' is safe for the pool-sharing reality including mobile.
judge_fix: Fig 9.8 caption (ch9-v6-p2): replace "thousands of homes share one public address" with "hundreds of homes share one public address".

quote: for almost exactly a hundred years it had been the right way to carry a voice
problem: 'Almost exactly' is more precise than the dates allow. The telephone was patented in 1876 and the first commercial exchange opened in 1878 (New Haven). That is 91 to 93 years before the 1969 ARPANET the chapter sets it against.
fix: "for nearly a hundred years it had been the right way to carry a voice"
reason: Telephone patent 1876, first commercial exchange 1878, versus 1969: about 91 to 93 years. 'Almost exactly' is more precise than the dates allow. The opener's 'a century' is fine.
judge_fix: ch9-circuits-p1: "for nearly a hundred years it had been the right way to carry a voice".

quote: set by the sender and verified nowhere along the path
problem: Fig 9.4's strip ('no router checks it') says the same. Both clash with the chapter's next sentence (most ISPs filter, BCP 38) and with Fig 9.10, which shows edge routers checking sources by uRPF. What is true is that IP itself has no check.
fix: ch9-security-p1: "is set by the sender and nothing in IP itself verifies it"; Fig 9.4 strip: "The sender writes it and IP itself never checks it, which is why a source address alone proves nothing."
reason: 'Verified nowhere along the path' is contradicted two sentences later by BCP 38 filtering and by Fig 9.10's edge check. The true claim is that IP itself has no check. Fig 9.4's 'no router checks it' has the same overstatement.
judge_fix: ch9-security-p1: "is set by the sender and nothing in IP itself verifies it". Fig 9.4 strip, 'The source': "The sender writes it and IP itself never checks it, which is why a source address alone proves nothing."

problem: ch9-ip-p1 'The first twenty bytes of a packet on the wire are the IP header': on an Ethernet wire the Ethernet header comes first, as Fig 8.11 draws it. The IP header opens the packet, not what is on the wire. It is also at least 20 bytes rather than exactly 20: options can take it to 60, which the strip's 'IHL ... almost always 5' admits while p1 says 'fixed-format'.
reason: On an Ethernet wire the frame header precedes the IP header, as the book's own Fig 8.11 draws it. 'Of a packet on the wire' is wrong, and the fix is two words. The 'at least 20 bytes' point is already covered by the strip's 'almost always 5', so only the wire wording needs fixing.
judge_fix: ch9-ip-p1: "The first twenty bytes of an IP packet are the *IP header*, a fixed-format arrangement of fields ..." (drop "on the wire").

problem: ch9-ip-p1 'every router on the path reads to figure out ... what the higher-layer protocol is': routers that only forward never use the Protocol field. The receiving host reads it to pass the payload to TCP or UDP. Routers look at it only when they filter traffic.
reason: Forwarding routers do not use the Protocol field. The receiving host reads it to hand the payload to TCP or UDP. The sentence has every router reading it.
judge_fix: ch9-ip-p1: replace "that every router on the path reads to figure out where the packet should go next, whether to fragment it, when to drop it, and what the higher-layer protocol is" with "whose fields tell each router on the path where the packet should go next, whether to fragment it and when to drop it, and tell the receiving host which higher-layer protocol the payload belongs to".

quote: The first twenty bytes of a packet on the wire are the IP header
problem: Chapter 8 (ch8-layers, Fig 8.x) has just shown an Ethernet header going in front of the IP header before the bits reach the wire, so the first bytes on the wire belong to the Ethernet header. A reader who took in that wrapping stops here. The same sentence also says every router reads the header to learn 'what the higher-layer protocol is'. Forwarding does not need that field; the receiver does.
fix: "The first twenty bytes of every IP packet (carried inside the Ethernet frame of Chapter 8) are the IP header, a fixed-format arrangement of fields that every router on the path reads to decide where the packet goes next, whether to fragment it and when to drop it; one field tells the receiver which higher-layer protocol the payload belongs to."
reason: Ch8 Fig 8.x (ch8-layers-p4 caption) puts an Ethernet header in front of the IP header, so the first bytes on the wire are not the IP header. The same sentence also lists 'the higher-layer protocol' among things a router reads to forward, but that field is for the receiver. Both points hold.
judge_fix: ch9-ip-p1: "The first twenty bytes of every IP packet (inside the Ethernet frame of Chapter 8) are the *IP header*, a fixed-format arrangement of fields that every router on the path reads to figure out where the packet should go next, whether to fragment it and when to drop it. One field tells the receiver which higher-layer protocol the payload belongs to." Rest of the paragraph unchanged.

quote: A 4000-byte packet meets a link that carries at most 1500
problem: The picture says '4000 bytes of data', and its fragments carry 1480 + 1480 + 1040 = 4000 data bytes, so the original packet is 4020 bytes. The caption calls it a 4000-byte packet, while the prose and the figure title say '4 KB', which a Part I reader may take as 4096. A reader who checks the strip's arithmetic (a 20-byte header on each piece) gets 3980 data bytes and cannot reach 1040.
fix: Caption: "A packet carrying 4000 bytes of data meets a link that carries at most 1500 bytes...". In ch9-ip-p3: "When a packet carrying 4000 bytes of data must traverse a 1500-byte link...". Figure title: "Fig 9.5 · 4000 bytes of data, fragmented onto a 1500-byte link".
reason: The picture says '4000 bytes of data' and 1480+1480+1040 = 4000 data bytes, so the original packet is 4020 bytes. The caption calls it a '4000-byte packet', and the prose and title say '4 KB', which a reader may take as 4096. All three disagree with the strip's arithmetic.
judge_fix: ch9-ip-p3: "When a packet carrying 4000 bytes of data must traverse a 1500-byte link...". Figure title and label: "Fig 9.5 · 4000 bytes of data, fragmented onto a 1500-byte link". The caption wording is in the fix for finding 11, which rewrites the same sentence. Both fixes must go in together.

quote: A more dramatic attack exploits BGP itself.
problem: The prose sets up hijacking as an attack ('the hijacker wins') and names Pakistan/YouTube as its canonical example. The Fig 9.11 strip then says 'No malice' and blames the spread on a leak upstream, and Fig 9.12 defines a route leak as 'nobody attacked anything'. The chapter never says what separates the two, so the reader cannot tell whether 2008 was a hijack, a leak or both.
fix: Open p4 with: "BGP can also be misled, by malice or by mistake." End p4 with: "This is BGP hijacking: announcing addresses you do not hold, whether on purpose or by error. The canonical example happened on 24 February 2008." In the Fig 9.12 caption, after 'route leak:', put: "the routes were genuine, but they reached a neighbour that should never have heard them."
reason: ch9-security-p4 calls the event an 'attack' by a 'hijacker', while the Fig 9.11 strip says 'No malice' and Fig 9.12 says 'nobody attacked anything'. The chapter never says that a hijack can be an honest mistake, or how it differs from a leak, so the reader cannot classify 2008.
judge_fix: ch9-security-p4 opening: "BGP can also be misled, by malice or by mistake." Last sentence: "This is *BGP hijacking*: announcing addresses you do not hold, whether on purpose or by error. The canonical example happened on *24 February 2008*." Fig 9.12 caption, before 'nobody attacked anything': "That is a **route leak**: the routes were genuine, but they reached a neighbour that should never have heard them; nobody attacked anything...". Keep the rest.

quote: the outage came from a configuration mistake upstream, where PCCW passed its customer's announcement on
problem: The chapter hero lead blames 'a misconfigured router in Pakistan' and says YouTube went off the air 'for the whole world'. The strip puts the only mistake at PCCW (Hong Kong), and the caption says 'almost everywhere'. Both companies erred: Pakistan Telecom sent its internal block route to PCCW, and PCCW passed it on unfiltered (RIPE NCC RIS case study, 2008).
fix: Strip: "No malice. The block was a domestic order; Pakistan Telecom's mistake was announcing the route to its upstream PCCW, and PCCW's was passing it on to the world without filtering it." Hero lead: "...for a misconfigured route from Pakistan to take YouTube off the air across most of the world for two hours."
reason: The Fig 9.11 strip puts the whole mistake at PCCW ('a configuration mistake upstream'). Per the RIPE NCC RIS case study, Pakistan Telecom's own error was announcing the internal block route to PCCW, and PCCW's was passing it on unfiltered. Both erred. The hero lead already says 'Pakistan's attempt to block YouTube at home to leak out ... almost everywhere', so only the strip needs the fix.
judge_fix: Fig 9.11 strip 'No malice': "The block was a domestic order. Pakistan Telecom's mistake was announcing the route to its upstream PCCW; PCCW's was passing it on to the world without filtering it." Leave the hero lead and caption as they are.

quote: each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table
problem: Ports first appear in Chapter 10 (ch10-udp). In Chapter 8 a 'port' was a physical socket on a switch (Fig 8.10), so a newcomer reads 'its own port' as a socket. NAT is never expanded, 'public address' is never set against a private one, and the prose of 05 never mentions CGNAT: the whole idea lives only in the caption.
fix: Add one clause to ch9-v6-p1 after the 2011 sentence: "Most ISPs stretched the old pool by putting many customers behind one public address, a trick called network address translation (Fig 9.8)." Caption: "...thousands of homes share one public address, and the NAT tells their connections apart by a port number (the connection label Chapter 10 introduces, not a socket on a switch) kept in a translation table."
reason: Network 'port' is first taught in Ch10 and Ch8 used 'port' for a switch socket. The Fig 9.8 caption leans on 'its own port' unexplained, and NAT is not expanded there. A newcomer will misread it. The finding's other proposal, a new sentence in p1 claiming 'most ISPs', is rejected as over-reach, since the section is one paragraph by design and the claim is not supported.
judge_fix: Fig 9.8 caption only: "...many ISPs put customers behind carrier-grade network address translation (**CGNAT**): thousands of homes share one public address, and each outgoing connection is given its own port number in a translation table (a label that tells connections apart, which Chapter 10 explains; not a socket on a switch)." Leave p1 alone.

quote: The internet is not one network. It is tens of thousands of independent networks
problem: This is the 'Not X. Y.' reveal the brief bans, used as the section's opening line.
fix: "The internet is tens of thousands of independent networks run by different organisations, glued together by a single protocol that lets them announce routes to one another."
reason: 'The internet is not one network. It is tens of thousands...' is the 'Not X. Y.' reveal that the pass brief bans outright.
judge_fix: ch9-routing-p1 opening: "The internet is tens of thousands of independent networks run by different organisations, glued together by a single protocol that lets them announce routes to one another." The rest of the paragraph is unchanged.

quote: Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.
problem: The h2 is three clipped dramatic fragments in a row. It also frames the ARPANET as a Cold War product, and the section's own last sentence denies that: ARPA built it 'to let universities share expensive computers, not to survive a war'. 'A Cold War' with the indefinite article reads oddly too.
fix: "Two letters, then a crash."
reason: 'Four nodes. A Cold War. The internet's first heartbeat.' is three clipped dramatic fragments, which the brief bans. 'A Cold War' also contradicts the section's closing line that ARPA built it to share computers, not to survive a war. The proposed 'Two letters, then a crash.' is another clipped pair, so use a plain title.
judge_fix: h2 of ch9-arpanet: "The first message, and the ideas behind it." Keep the section id and anchors. The label '02 · ARPANET 1969' is unchanged.

quote: was tasked in 1966 with building an experimental network, by 1967 he had read all three sets of work
problem: The sentence starts 'When X was tasked in 1966...' and continues 'by 1967 he had read', which breaks the syntax. It then keeps going through two nested parentheticals to 'the network's first routers', so the reader has to read it twice.
fix: "In 1966 ARPA (the US Advanced Research Projects Agency, not yet renamed DARPA) tasked Larry Roberts with building an experimental network. By 1967 he had read all three sets of work, and the design that emerged was Baran's mesh, Davies's terminology and Kleinrock's math. The firm Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) built its IMPs (Interface Message Processors), the network's first routers."
reason: 'When Larry Roberts ... was tasked in 1966 ..., by 1967 he had read ...' has no main clause after 'When', so the syntax is broken. The following nested parentheticals make it worse.
judge_fix: ch9-arpanet-p3, from 'When Larry Roberts': "In 1966 Larry Roberts at ARPA (the US Advanced Research Projects Agency, not yet renamed DARPA) was tasked with building an experimental network. By 1967 he had read all three sets of work, and the design that emerged was unmistakably Baran's mesh, Davies's terminology and Kleinrock's math. The firm Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) built the IMPs (Interface Message Processors), the network's first routers." Then keep 'The "LO" message was packet switching going live...'.

quote: a packet network shares every link, and each packet finds its own way, sometimes arriving out of order
problem: The caption says again what p2 and p3 just explained (circuits held through the silences, shared links, packets finding their own way and arriving out of order, computers talking in bursts). The strip's 'Putting it back' repeats p3's 'numbered chunks... reassembles them'. The brief says the prose keeps it and the caption names the picture.

quote: Its first message, on 29 October, went from UCLA to SRI: L and O arrived, then the receiving system crashed.

quote: IANA handed out its last blocks of IPv4 addresses on 3 February 2011

quote: which is why, three decades on, the move is still unfinished
problem: p1 says the migration is unfinished 'structurally': a v6-only and a v4-only machine cannot talk, so nobody can drop v4 until nearly everyone has v6. This strip restates the same conclusion with a different cause (every router and OS had to change). The reader gets two 'why's for one fact.
fix: "The price. Every router, operating system, firewall and networking library had to change before IPv6 could carry real traffic."
reason: ch9-v6-p1 gives the structural reason the migration is unfinished: v6-only and v4-only machines cannot talk. The Fig 9.9 strip 'The price' gives a different cause with 'which is why', so the reader gets two competing 'why's for one fact. The cost is real, but it is not the stated reason.
judge_fix: Fig 9.9 strip: "*The price.* Every router, operating system, firewall and networking library had to change before IPv6 could carry real traffic."

quote: The sender writes the source address itself and routers forward on the destination alone
problem: The unchecked source field is explained three times: the Fig 9.4 strip ('The sender writes it and no router checks it'), p1, and this caption. The edge filter has three names (BCP 38 in p1, 'source address validation' here, uRPF in the strip) that are never tied together, so a newcomer may think there are three defences. 'Uneven' is said in p1 ('enforcement is uneven. Spoofed packets still flow.') and again in the strip ('Uneven deployment').

Strip: "Automating the check. Routers can apply BCP 38 automatically (uRPF)...". Cut the strip item 'Uneven deployment' or cut p1's 'Spoofed packets still flow.' Cut the Fig 9.4 strip item 'The source', since section 06 teaches it.

The ISP-edge defence appears under three names (BCP 38, 'source address validation', uRPF) that are never tied together. 'Uneven' appears in p1 and in the strip. The strip item cites CAIDA Spoofer, which p1 lacks, so keep the strip version and cut p1's.
judge_fix: Fig 9.10 caption: "The same forged packet twice: with no filter at the ISP's edge it gets through and any reply goes to the address it names; with the BCP 38 check on, the edge router drops it, because the source is not one of the customer's own addresses." Strip 'Automating the check': "Routers can apply BCP 38 automatically: strict unicast reverse path forwarding (uRPF) accepts a packet only if the route back to its source leaves through the interface the packet arrived on." ch9-security-p1: cut 'Spoofed packets still flow.' Cut the Fig 9.4 strip item 'The source', since section 06 teaches it.

quote: ToS once meant priority and now carries DSCP and ECN
problem: These are two acronyms that are never explained and never used again: expert detail the baseline reader cannot carry.
fix: "ToS once meant priority and now carries traffic-class and congestion marks"
reason: DSCP and ECN are named with no gloss, and nothing in Chapter 9 uses either. Ch10 does explain ECN ('lets routers mark packets instead of dropping them'). This is expert detail the baseline reader cannot hold (law 4). A plain gloss plus a pointer to Ch10 fixes it.
judge_fix: Fig 9.4 strip: "**ToS** once meant priority; today it marks a traffic class and congestion (ECN, met in Chapter 10)". Keep the rest of the item.

quote: The TTL drops by one at every hop; if it reaches 0 the router drops the packet and reports back
problem: The caption already says each router lowers the TTL by one and recomputes the checksum, and the strip says both again. Neither says why the field exists (so that a packet caught in a routing loop dies instead of circling forever), so the mechanism arrives without its purpose.
fix: "Time to live. It exists so that a packet caught in a routing loop dies instead of circling forever: at 0 the router drops it and reports back, which is how traceroute maps a path... The checksum covers only the header, which is why changing the TTL forces a new one."
reason: The strip says what TTL does and how traceroute uses it, but never why it exists. The purpose (a packet in a routing loop must die) is the reason the mechanism is there, and it is missing.
judge_fix: Fig 9.4 strip 'Time to live': "The **TTL** drops by one at every hop, so a packet caught in a routing loop eventually dies; at 0 the router drops it and reports back, which is how `traceroute` maps a path: probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 make each hop answer in turn. The checksum covers only the header, so each hop recomputes it."

quote: The Cuban Missile Crisis had just shown the world how close to thermonuclear war it was
problem: Baran's work is dated 1960 to 1964, and 'had just shown' puts the crisis before that work began. The crisis was October 1962, midway through it.

judge_fix: ch9-arpanet-p2: "In October 1962, midway through that work, the Cuban Missile Crisis showed the world how close to thermonuclear war it was; the existing AT&T long-distance telephone network..."

quote: That is 4 294 967 296 possible addresses, which sounded like a lot in 1981, and fewer are usable

fix: "That is 4,294,967,296 possible addresses, which sounded like a lot in 1981. Fewer are usable: whole ranges are reserved, and blocks are handed out in fixed sizes, so part of each often sits idle."

judge_fix: ch9-v6-p1: "IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long. That is 4,294,967,296 possible addresses, which sounded like a lot in 1981, though fewer are usable: whole ranges are reserved, and blocks are handed out in fixed sizes, so part of each often sits idle."

quote: There are no reservations, no setup phase, no central authority that has to grant a circuit before traffic flows.
problem: This is a reflexive triplet: 'no reservations' and 'no setup phase' are the same fact. In circuit switching it is the switches, not a 'central authority', that set up the circuit.
fix: "Nothing has to be reserved or set up before traffic flows."
reason: 'no reservations, no setup phase, no central authority' is a reflexive triplet whose first two items are the same fact. 'Central authority' is also inaccurate for circuit switching, where the switches themselves set up the path (p1).
judge_fix: ch9-circuits-p3 last sentence: "Nothing has to be reserved or set up before traffic flows."

quote: which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood relies on it

quote: A 4000-byte packet meets a link that carries at most 1500
problem: The picture and desc show a packet carrying 4000 bytes of data, and the fragments carry 1480 + 1480 + 1040 = 4000 data bytes. That makes the original packet 4020 bytes with its header. A '4000-byte packet' would leave 3980 data bytes and a last fragment of 1020. Anyone checking against the How it works arithmetic finds a 20-byte mismatch.
fix: "A packet carrying 4000 bytes of data meets a link that carries at most 1500, so it is cut into three fragments, each with the same ID, its offset (in 8-byte units) and a more-fragments flag."
reason: The figure and strip show 4000 bytes of data (1480+1480+1040) plus a 20-byte header per fragment, so the original packet is 4020 bytes. The caption's '4000-byte packet' is 20 bytes off for anyone who checks the strip's arithmetic. The title and p3 say '4 KB', which is loose enough to be fine. Low severity.
judge_fix: Caption (ch9-ip-p4): "A packet carrying 4000 bytes of data meets a link that carries at most 1500, so it is cut into three fragments, each with the same ID, its offset (in 8-byte units) and a more-fragments flag. Lose any one and the receiver must throw the whole packet away, since IP cannot ask for a single fragment again."

quote: thousands of homes share one public address
problem: One IPv4 address has 65,535 ports. Carrier-grade NAT usually hands each subscriber a block of several hundred to a few thousand ports, so one public address serves dozens of customers (often 16 to 64), not thousands. A reader who knows networking stops here.
fix: "many ISPs put customers behind carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT): dozens of homes share one public address, each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table."
reason: Checked on the web. Vendor and ISP guidance for CGNAT clusters at about 64:1 to 128:1 subscribers per public IPv4 address (Purple, NFWare, ZCorum). Another source puts it at 50 to 200. Mobile networks run higher. 'Thousands of homes' overstates the typical case, and the figure shows three homes. Sources: https://nfware.com/blog/how-many-subscribers-can-be-behind-one-ipv4-address , https://www.zcorum.com/solutions/cgnat/roi-calculation/ , https://test-ipv6.run/faq/ipv6-behind-cgnat
judge_fix: Caption (ch9-v6-p2): "Since the free pool of IPv4 addresses ran out in 2011, many ISPs put customers behind carrier-grade NAT (**CGNAT**): dozens or hundreds of homes share one public address, each outgoing connection given its own port in a translation table."

quote: IPv6 · 128 bits · about 3.4 × 10³⁸
problem: The exponent uses Unicode superscripts. At 375 px it renders as '10³ ⁸': the ³ comes from Space Mono and the ⁸ from a fallback font. The two glyphs differ in size, sit a gap apart, and are about 5 CSS px tall, below the 11 px floor in law 3. This is the figure's key number.
fix: Draw the exponent as a tspan in the figure font: `about 3.4 × 10<tspan dy="-5" font-size="12.5">38</tspan>` (12.5 × 357/400 ≈ 11.2 px rendered). Or write "about 3.4 × 10^38", the form the How it works strip uses.
reason: The t=5.333 screenshot shows '10³⁸' as two tiny glyphs from mixed fonts, far smaller than the 13 px label around them and under the 11 px floor in law 3. It is the figure's key number. The How it works strip uses the sup form, which is fine.
judge_fix: In the figure label, replace the Unicode superscripts with a tspan in the figure font: about 3.4 × 10<tspan dy="-5" font-size="12">38</tspan>. Add a dy="5" tspan afterwards only if text follows. If the generator cannot do tspans, write "about 3.4 × 10^38", the form the desc uses. Keep the rendered size at 11 px or more at 375 px width.

quote: Flags 010
problem: The value 010 (the don't-fragment bit set) is shown, but nothing in the figure, its strip or the chapter decodes it. Part 3 never mentions don't-fragment. A newcomer is left holding a mark they cannot read. Fig 9.5 explains only the more-fragments flag.

To keep the empty reserved wire on screen for about 1.5 s, delay voice dots 7 and 8 by about 0.1 of the cycle, or stretch the cycle to 9 to 10 s so they do not wrap.
